title: Missing Local 208 funds, Hal Davis and Saunders's union role
summary: Only $38,000 and a building were handed over of a reported $250,000; Price Waterhouse could not account for it; Saunders served as assistant to Barney Richards with Leon Washington as business agent.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Was that because -- I don't know, in your opinion, or do you know, it was because of money that he had coming, and by being president of this local, under the table stuff, or --
Well, --
Or was he really concerned about the investments of 208?

No, they couldn't have been, because the way they negotiated, they -- there was a lot of money missing, when they finally were going to merge. They were supposed to have turned over all the assets. They only turned over $38,000 in cash money. And then they had a building, so they turned this building over and $38,000. But they were talking figures of $250,000.
What happened to that money?
Well, this is what I'm saying. Now, there again, Price Waterhouse examined their books, 208, and come back with the conclusion that they couldn't give an accurate accounting.
So the Federation stepped in to save Local 208's face, and sent their auditor. And he gave them a clean bill

of goods. So that -- I mean, it goes to show you how these things have worked out from the higher-ups. And -- but they're doing it to protect each other, and they didn't want any -- they didn't want the waters to be ruffled at all.
In fact, a trustee of Local 10 for that period was Hal Davis.
Hal C. Davis, right.
He became president of International --
Of International.
-- and just recently died.
Yeah, recently died, right, right.
Yeah, I met him at that time, because we were covering the story.
Yeah, right, right.
And --

See, and at this time, I was an assistant to Barney Richards, and Leon Washington came in as a business agent, see, so that to be -- have some representation for the musicians who had come in before. Now, all of this is before the merger. See, this is before the merger. And so we were -- and then this is when the trusteeship and Hal Davis came in.
In fact, I came over to the union that day that you and the rest of the guys came in.
Right, right, right, right. I have
pictures and things of that, the news and the lawyers and all of that.
The union is something else. It has nothing at all to do with music, of course.
No.
